analysis.one_liner: Forces health insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and drug wholesalers to sell off any doctors' practices, pharmacies, or clinics they own.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one Democrat and one Republican, the bill has received no action since being referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for a company to own both a health insurer or pharmacy benefit manager and medical providers like doctors' practices, pharmacies, or hospitals — and illegal for a drug or device wholesaler to own providers. Any company in that situation would have one year to sell off one side of the business, with 10% of its profits moved into escrow each month if it misses milestones. The bill also lets federal agencies, state attorneys general, and individual patients sue to enforce the breakup, with triple damages for patients who were overcharged.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay more for drugs and care at company-owned pharmacies and physician practices; taxpayers, because the bill's findings describe insurers using employed physicians to inflate Medicare Advantage payments; independent physicians and community pharmacies that compete against arms of insurance conglomerates; and state attorneys general, who gain a new enforcement tool. Disgorged revenue from violators would go into a fund for the overcharged communities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, taxpayers, independent doctors and pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: It would break up vertical integration in health care: a company could no longer own both an insurance plan or pharmacy benefit manager and the doctors, pharmacies, or hospitals it steers patients toward. Divestment would be due within one year of enactment [S2].

The bill's findings cite the scale of the problem: the three largest pharmacy benefit managers process nearly 80% of prescription drug claims and are each part of a large health care platform; one insurer conglomerate employs about 10% of all American physicians; and the three largest drug wholesalers control 98% of U.S. drug distribution [S2].

It targets conflicts of interest the bill says the FTC has documented: integrated pharmacy benefit managers steer business to their own pharmacies, raising drug costs, and insurers game the Medical Loss Ratio profit cap by hiding profits in unregulated pharmacy or physician units [S2].

Enforcement has teeth: monthly escrow of 10% of profits for missing divestment milestones, a court-appointed trustee who can force a sale, civil suits by the FTC, the Justice Department, HHS's Inspector General, and state attorneys general, and a private right of action for patients with treble damages and attorney's fees [S2].
Money taken from violators through disgorgement would go into an FTC-administered fund for the harmed community, including consumers overcharged at vertically integrated conglomerates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The vertically integrated health care conglomerates — insurers that own pharmacy benefit managers and physician networks, the big three drug wholesalers that have been buying specialty practices, and the management services organizations that channel doctors into corporate ownership. They would have to sell off multibillion-dollar business lines within a year, and face profit escrow, divestiture trustees, and treble-damage lawsuits if they do not. Indirectly, any savings for consumers depend on new competition actually emerging after divestitures.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big insurance, PBM, and drug wholesaler conglomerates

drawbacks.text: The one-year forced divestment clock is unusually fast for assets of this size. Buyers would have to be found quickly for large physician networks, pharmacies, and specialty practices, and a rushed sale process could disrupt care for patients mid-treatment or leave divested entities financially shaky despite the required FTC and DOJ review of each divestiture [S2].

Defenders of integration argue owning pharmacies and physician practices can lower costs and coordinate care, and the bill would unwind deals even where integration produced real efficiencies; the bill does not include an efficiency exception, only a review of each divestiture's effect on competition, financial viability, and the public interest [S2].

The bill's definitions are broad: 'provider' sweeps in everything from inpatient pharmacies to hospitals, and 'management services organization' covers many standard business arrangements with practices, so the prohibition reaches far beyond the largest conglomerates and would generate litigation over edge cases [S2].

A private right of action with treble damages invites a wave of class-action litigation in parallel with the FTC, DOJ, and state enforcement, which could add legal costs throughout the health sector during the transition [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains are large and well-documented in the bill's own findings: an insurance-PBM-provider complex that steers patients, inflates Medicare Advantage payments, and hides profits from rate regulation now touches most American medical care. The main honest cost is transition risk — divesting that much of the health system within one year will be disruptive, and the bill bets that competition, not just breakup, follows. The design mitigates this with escrowed profits returned if deadlines are met, trustee-supervised sales, and case-by-case review of buyers, but execution would be the hardest part.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sits with no hearing, vote, or movement so far.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Break Up Big Medicine Act on February 10, 2026, 'for herself and Mr. Hawley,' giving it a Republican cosponsor from the start [S2].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, the standard first step that sends a bill to the committee with jurisdiction over it [S4].
The cosponsor list shows exactly one cosponsor, Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican [S3].
Since the referral, the action history shows no committee hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so the vertically integrated health conglomerates keep their current structure and their position in the market. A bill forcing them to divest tens of billions of dollars in holdings has advanced no further than a committee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, the health conglomerates, unchanged

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Break Up Big Medicine Act and sponsored it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators are on record, one from each party — Sen. Warren (D) and Sen. Hawley (R) — and no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape of the full Senate is unknown.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated insurance and PBM conglomerates (e.g., insurers that own PBMs, pharmacies, and physician networks)
industries.note: These companies would be barred from owning both the insurance or PBM side and the providers on the other side, and would have one year to divest. The bill's findings say their integrated model lets them steer patients, evade profit caps, and inflate Medicare Advantage payments [S2].

The three largest PBMs, which process nearly 80% of drug claims and are each tied to a large health platform, would have to separate from any provider ownership, and the bill's definition covers PBMs even if they call themselves something else [S2].
The three largest wholesalers control 98% of drug distribution and have been acquiring specialty practices; the bill makes that combination unlawful and forces divestiture of the provider side [S2].

industries.industry: Corporate physician groups and management services organizations
industries.note: MSOs are the structure through which corporate owners control physician practices, and the bill treats an insurer or wholesaler owning or controlling an MSO the same as owning the provider directly [S2].

industries.industry: Independent physician practices and community pharmacies
industries.note: These providers compete against subsidiaries of insurance conglomerates that can steer patients to their own pharmacies and doctors; forced divestiture would shrink that advantage [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills like this rarely move on their own: with only two Senate sponsors, no hearing or markup scheduled, and referral to the Judiciary Committee, the most likely path is that it sits untouched and expires at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027. Its realistic hope is being folded into a larger health care or antitrust package, or revived in a future Congress.
